To determine whether lung cancer is more likely than its absence overall, we must calculate the total probability of having lung cancer ($P(\text{Lung Cancer})$) based on the provided conditional probabilities and the prevalence of smoking.

    *   $P(\text{Smoker}) = 0.12$
    *   $P(\text{Non-Smoker}) = 1 - 0.12 = 0.88$
    *   $P(\text{Lung Cancer} \mid \text{Non-Smoker}) = 0.58$
    *   $P(\text{Lung Cancer} \mid \text{Smoker}) = 0.61$

This is an unusually high baseline rate compared to real-world statistics, but in the context of this hypothetical world defined by the professor, we must strictly adhere to these numbers regardless of their realism.*

2.  **Calculate the total probability of lung cancer using the Law of Total Probability:**
    $$P(\text{Lung Cancer}) = P(\text{Lung Cancer} \mid \text{Non-Smoker}) \times P(\text{Non-Smoker}) + P(\text{Lung Cancer} \mid \text{Smoker}) \times P(\text{Smoker})$$

    Substituting the values:
    $$P(\text{Lung Cancer}) = (0.58 \times 0.88) + (0.61 \times 0.12)$$

    *   Contribution from nonsmokers: $0.58 \times 0.88 = 0.5104$

    $$P(\text{Lung Cancer}) = 0.5104 + 0.0732 = 0.5836$$

    *   $P(\text{Lung Cancer}) = 0.5836$ (or 58.36%)
    *   $P(\text{No Lung Cancer}) = 1 - P(\text{Lung Cancer}) = 1 - 0.5836 = 0.4164$ (or 41.64%)

Since $0.5836 > 0.4164$, lung cancer is indeed more likely than its absence in this specific hypothetical world.
